summary: Gives examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) call flows, including registration and session establishment. It shows call flow diagrams and message details among user agents, proxy servers and redirect servers. It is a best current practice document.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP is the protocol that sets up internet phone calls. This document shows the actual messages exchanged for the everyday cases: registering a phone, calling another phone, calling through a proxy, and calling someone who is busy or does not answer.

questions: what is a sip call flow
what does sip invite 180 ringing 200 ok ack mean
subtitle: Worked examples of how SIP calls are set up, from registering a phone to handling a call that fails.

tldr.problem: The SIP specification says what each message means, but a lot of the practice lies in how those messages are put together: which server asks for credentials, which one records the route, how a failure is reported back.
tldr.mechanism: The document works through a series of scenarios, from registering a user agent to calling one directly, through two proxies, through an application layer gateway, and through a call that is cancelled, refused or never answered. Each scenario is given as a diagram and the full text of every message.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3665 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. It warns that the flows illustrate good practice but must not be copied literally, because some details were simplified for the sake of reading them.

today: RFC 3665 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 75, and has not been obsoleted. It is a companion to the SIP specification in RFC 3261, and the document says plainly that its flows illustrate good practice but should not be copied literally, because some details were simplified to make them readable.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The call flows shown in this document were developed in the design of a SIP IP communications network, and they represent an example minimum set of functionality. The hope of the authors is that the document will be useful for SIP implementers, designers and protocol researchers alike, and will help further the goal of a standard implementation of the SIP specification.

These flows are based on version 2.0 of SIP in RFC 3261, with SDP usage described in RFC 3264. Other RFCs also comprise the SIP standard but are not used in this set of basic call flows. Call flow examples of SIP interworking with the PSTN through gateways are contained in a companion document, RFC 3666.
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP specification is precise about each message but leaves plenty of choices to the implementer. This document fills in those choices by showing complete worked examples, and it is a companion to the specification rather than a replacement for it.

sections.title: Assumptions and How to Read the Flows
sections.content:
A number of architecture, network and protocol assumptions underlie the call flows. These assumptions are not requirements, and they are outlined so that they may be taken into consideration and to aid understanding. Authentication of SIP user agents in the examples is performed using HTTP Digest, and some proxy servers insert Record-Route headers into requests to ensure that they are in the signaling path for future message exchanges. The flows show TCP, TLS and UDP for transport.

The document does not prescribe the flows precisely as they are shown, but rather the flows illustrate the principles for best practice. They are best practice usages of SIP methods, headers and parameters. The exact flows must not be copied as they are by an implementer, because specific incorrect characteristics were introduced into the document for convenience. For simplicity in reading and editing there are a number of differences between the examples and actual SIP messages: the HTTP Digest responses are not actual MD5 encodings, Call-IDs are often repeated, CSeq counts often begin at 1, header fields are usually shown in the same order, and usually only the minimum required header field set is shown, so others that would normally be present, such as Accept, Supported and Allow, are not shown.

The legend says that dashed lines represent signaling messages that are mandatory to the call scenario and the arrow indicates the direction of flow, double dashed lines represent media paths between network elements, and messages with parentheses around their name are optional. Messages are identified in the figures as F1, F2 and so on, which references the message details in the list that follows the figure.
sections.plainLanguage: Read the diagrams as a sketch of who talks to whom and in what order, not as a template to copy. The document deliberately shortens the messages, so a real implementation will need the full header set and real digests.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content:
Registration binds a particular device contact URI with a SIP user address of record. The first scenario is a successful new registration: Bob sends a REGISTER request to the SIP server, the request includes the user's contact list, the server provides a challenge, Bob's client answers it, the server validates the credentials, registers the user in its contact database and returns 200 OK with the user's current contact list in Contact headers. The flow shows HTTP Digest for authentication over TLS transport, which is used because of the lack of integrity protection in HTTP Digest and the danger of registration hijacking without it.

The remaining registration scenarios are variations on the same exchange. When Bob updates his contact list he supplies credentials with the request and is not challenged again, because he has already authenticated. When Bob wants the current contact list he sends a REGISTER with no Contact headers and the server answers 200 OK with the list. To cancel a registration Bob sends a REGISTER with an expiration period of 0 applying to all existing contact locations, and the server clears the contact list. In the unsuccessful case the credentials do not match and the server answers 401 Unauthorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering tells the server where your phone can be reached. The server asks for a password the first time and remembers you afterwards, so later registrations go straight through. Setting the expiry to zero is how you log out.

sections.title: A Call Between Two User Agents
sections.content:
Session establishment is detailed between two SIP user agents, Alice and Bob, assumed to be SIP phones or SIP-enabled devices. The successful calls show the initial signaling, the exchange of media information in the form of SDP payloads, the establishment of the media session, and finally the termination of the call. HTTP Digest authentication is used by proxy servers to authenticate the caller Alice, and it is assumed that Bob has registered with the proxy server as described in the registration section, so that he can receive calls through it.

In the simplest scenario Alice completes a call to Bob directly. She sends an INVITE, Bob answers with 180 Ringing, then with 200 OK, Alice acknowledges with an ACK, and the two-way RTP media flows between them. The call ends when one side sends a BYE and the other answers 200 OK.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller offers a call, the other end says it is ringing, then accepts, the caller acknowledges, and the conversation starts. Either side can end it with a BYE, which the other side confirms.

sections.title: Calls Through Proxies and Redirect Servers
sections.content:
In the two-proxy scenario Alice completes a call to Bob using proxy 1 and proxy 2. The initial INVITE contains a pre-loaded Route header with the address of proxy 1, which is configured as a default outbound proxy for Alice. The request does not contain the credentials proxy 1 requires, so a 407 Proxy Authorization response is sent containing the challenge information, and a new INVITE is then sent containing the correct credentials. The call terminates when Bob disconnects by initiating a BYE. Proxy 1 inserts a Record-Route header into the INVITE to ensure that it is present in all subsequent message exchanges, and proxy 2 also inserts itself into that header. The ACK and BYE both have a Route header.

Other scenarios cover a session with multiple proxy authentication, a session with proxy failure, and a session via redirect and proxy servers with SDP in the ACK. In the proxy failure scenario Alice is configured for a primary and a secondary SIP proxy server, or is able to use DNS SRV records to locate them, and has valid credentials for both domains. Proxy 1 is out of service and does not respond to INVITEs, being reachable but unresponsive, so Alice completes the call to Bob using proxy 2. In the redirect scenario the INVITE is first sent to a redirect server, which returns a 302 Moved Temporarily response containing a Contact header with Bob's current SIP address; Alice then generates a new INVITE and sends it via the proxy server. In that example no SDP is present in the INVITE, so the SDP is carried in the ACK message.
sections.plainLanguage: Most calls do not go straight to the other phone. A proxy sits in the path and forwards the messages, and it may insist on a password before it will do so. A redirect server does something different: it simply tells the caller a new address to try, and the caller starts again from scratch.

sections.title: Media Paths and the Application Layer Gateway
sections.content:
In the application layer gateway scenario Alice completes a call to Bob through an ALG and a SIP proxy. The routing through the ALG is accomplished using a pre-loaded Route header in the INVITE. The media stream setup is not end-to-end: the ALG terminates both media streams and bridges them. This is done by the ALG modifying the SDP in the INVITE and the 200 OK messages, and possibly any 18x or ACK messages containing SDP. In addition to firewall traversal, this back-to-back user agent could be used as part of an anonymizer service, in which all identifying information on Alice would be removed, or to perform codec media conversion, such as mu-law to A-law conversion of PCM on an international call. Proxy 2 does not Record-Route in this call flow.

A separate example shows a session in which the media changes midway through. When Bob's IP address changes during the session, Bob sends a re-INVITE containing new Contact and SDP information with an incremented version number. In that flow the proxy does not Record-Route, so it is not in the SIP messaging path after the initial exchange, and a new RTP media stream is established.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the two phones cannot send sound directly to each other, and a gateway in between receives the sound and passes it on. It rewrites the description of the media so that each side talks to the gateway rather than to the other, and it can also translate between different audio encodings.

sections.title: Calls That Do Not Succeed
sections.content:
Four scenarios cover calls that fail. In the no-answer scenario Alice gives up before Bob answers, sending a CANCEL because no final response had been received from Bob; if a 200 OK to the INVITE had crossed with the CANCEL, Alice would have sent an ACK and then a BYE to properly terminate the call. The CANCEL message is acknowledged with a 200 OK on a hop by hop basis rather than end to end.

In the busy scenario Bob is busy and sends a 486 Busy Here response to Alice's INVITE, and the non-2xx response is acknowledged on a hop-by-hop basis instead of end-to-end. The document notes that many SIP user agents will not return a 486 response, as they have multiple line and other features.

In the no-response scenario there is no response from Bob to the INVITE messages being re-transmitted by proxy 2, and after the sixth re-transmission proxy 2 gives up and sends a 480 No Response to Alice. In the temporarily unavailable scenario Bob initially sends a 180 Ringing response to Alice, indicating that alerting is taking place, but then a 480 Unavailable is sent, which is acknowledged and proxied back to Alice.
sections.plainLanguage: A call can fail in several ways, and the failure has to travel back along the same path the offer came along. If the caller changes its mind before the other end answers, it sends a cancel. If nobody answers at all, the proxy eventually gives up and reports that there was no response.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since the document contains examples of SIP session establishment, the security considerations in the SIP specification apply. That specification describes the basic threats including registration hijacking, server impersonation, message body tampering, session modifying or teardown, and denial of service and amplification attacks.

The use of HTTP Digest as shown in the document provides one-way authentication and protection against replay attacks. TLS transport is used in registration scenarios because of the lack of integrity protection in HTTP Digest and the danger of registration hijacking without it. The use of TLS and the Secure SIP, sips, URI scheme provides a better level of security including two-way authentication. S/MIME can provide end-to-end confidentiality and integrity protection of message bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples protect the caller with a one-way password check and, during registration, with an encrypted connection. The document points out that a stronger option exists for people who need the ends of the call to be authenticated to each other.
